title: Given a string s and a pattern p, determine whether s contains any permutation of p as a contiguous substring. Solve it with the fixed-size sliding window pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Challenge 1: Permutation in a String (Does s Contain a Permutation of p)

s1_definition.profdef: This problem asks whether any contiguous substring of the source string s of length equal to the pattern p is an anagram of p, meaning it uses exactly the same characters with exactly the same counts in any order. It is solved with a fixed-size sliding window of width equal to the pattern length, comparing the window's character-count signature against the pattern's signature using a matched counter so each slide is constant time. It runs in linear time.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh has a required set of approval stamps for a loan file, say two manager stamps and one auditor stamp, in no particular order. He scans a long ledger of stamps applied over time and wants to know if any consecutive block of exactly three stamps happens to be exactly that required set in some order. He slides a fixed three-wide window across the ledger and checks each block's stamp counts against the required counts.
s1_definition.oneliner: Slide a fixed-width window the size of the pattern and check whether its character counts ever exactly match the pattern's counts.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem asks whether any contiguous substring of the source string s of length equal to the pattern p is an anagram of p, meaning it uses exactly the same characters with exactly the same counts in any order. It is solved with a fixed-size sliding window of width equal to the pattern length, comparing the window's character-count signature against the pattern's signature using a matched counter so each slide is constant time. It runs in linear time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh has a required set of approval stamps for a loan file, say two manager stamps and one auditor stamp, in no particular order. He scans a long ledger of stamps applied over time and wants to know if any consecutive block of exactly three stamps happens to be exactly that required set in some order. He slides a fixed three-wide window across the ledger and checks each block's stamp counts against the required counts.

**One line to remember:** Slide a fixed-width window the size of the pattern and check whether its character counts ever exactly match the pattern's counts.

sections.s2_technical:
We first build a count signature of the pattern, for example an `int[26]` for lowercase letters or a `HashMap<Character,Integer>` for a general alphabet, recording how many times each character appears in p. We then create a window count of the same shape for the first p-length characters of s. The question reduces to whether the window count ever equals the pattern count as the window slides across s.

Comparing two full count arrays on every slide would cost the alphabet size per step, which is wasteful. The efficient approach uses a matched counter. We precompute how many distinct characters the pattern needs and maintain a counter `matches` for how many of those characters currently have exactly the right count in the window. When a character enters the window we increment its window count, and if that count becomes equal to the required count we increment matches, but if it becomes one more than required we decrement matches because it just moved away from a match. When a character leaves the window we do the mirror image: decrement its window count, incrementing matches if it just reached the required count and decrementing matches if it just dropped below from an exact match.

With that bookkeeping, the window contains a permutation of the pattern exactly when matches equals the number of distinct required characters. We check this condition after forming the first window and after every slide. For example `if (matches == required) return true;`. The senior-level nuance is that the matched counter turns each slide into constant work regardless of alphabet size, which is the difference between an O(n times alphabet) solution and a clean O(n) solution.

The time complexity is linear, O(s + p), since we build the pattern signature once and then perform a constant amount of work per slide across s. The space complexity is O(alphabet size), bounded and effectively constant. This fixed-size window with a matched counter is the standard efficient template for anagram-search problems.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, loan files require a specific set of approval stamps in specific quantities, for example two manager approvals and one auditor approval, but the order in which they are applied does not matter. The approvals audit system stores, for each file, the chronological ledger of stamp codes applied. Compliance wants to know whether at any point a consecutive block of stamps exactly equal in size to the required set was applied that forms a complete valid approval set in some order, because that proves the file was properly approved within a single contiguous approval session. This is exactly the permutation-in-a-string problem.

Problem 2 — Comparing counts from scratch for every possible block is wasteful across the bank's large volume of loan files. The fixed-size window with a matched counter gives constant work per slide and a single linear pass per ledger, which keeps the compliance scan fast.

The code has the shared `Account` class, an `ApprovalLedgerScanner` service with a `containsCompleteApprovalSet` method implementing the fixed window with a matched counter, and a runnable `PermutationInStringDemo` main class that scans Rajesh's and Priya's ledgers for the required stamp set, logging matches at fine level and the final answer at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's ledger "AMMAX" with required "MMA", which needs two M and one A, giving two distinct requirements. The window width is 3. We keep a window count map and a matches counter at 0.

Step 1: Right at index 0, character A. A is needed, window A becomes 1, which equals required 1, matches becomes 1. Window not yet full width, matches is 1, not 2.

Step 2: Right at index 1, character M. Window M becomes 1, required is 2, not equal, matches stays 1. Window still only two wide.

Step 3: Right at index 2, character M. Window M becomes 2, equals required 2, matches becomes 2. Window is now exactly three wide, indices 0 to 2, "AMM", and matches equals 2 which equals the requirements, so a permutation is found. Wait, "AMM" has two M and one A, which is indeed a permutation of "MMA". So the answer is true at block start index 0.

The scanner returns true: the block "AMM" at indices 0 to 2 is a permutation of the required set "MMA".

```

2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Complete approval set found at block start 0
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Ledger 'AMMAX' contains required set 'MMA' = true
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Rajesh Kumar approved in one session = true
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Ledger 'MAXMA' contains required set 'MMA' = false
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Priya Sharma approved in one session = false

    │ window={}, matches=0

    ├─ r=0 'A' winA1=need matches1              block="A"
    ├─ r=1 'M' winM1 (need2) matches1           block="AM"

  Output: true  (contiguous block "AMM" is a permutation of "MMA")
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem asks whether a source string contains any permutation of a pattern as a contiguous substring, and I solve it with a fixed-size sliding window whose width equals the pattern length, running in linear time. I build a count signature of the pattern, then slide a window of exactly that width across the source. A block is a permutation of the pattern exactly when its character counts match the pattern's counts, so my job is to detect, efficiently, whenever the window's counts equal the pattern's counts.

The efficient trick I always describe is the matched counter. Instead of comparing whole count arrays on every slide, I keep a count of how many required characters currently have exactly the right amount in the window. When a character enters I bump that count toward or away from a match, and when a character leaves the window I apply the mirror update, so each slide is constant work. The window holds a permutation precisely when the matched counter equals the number of distinct required characters, which I check after each slide.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the approvals audit system. Loan files required a specific set of approval stamps in specific quantities but in any order, and for each file we stored the chronological ledger of stamps applied. We checked whether any contiguous block of stamps exactly the size of the required set formed a complete valid approval set in some order, because that proved the file was properly approved within a single contiguous approval session. The fixed window with a matched counter gave constant work per slide and one linear pass per ledger.

The senior-level point I make is that the matched counter is what separates a sloppy O(n times alphabet) solution from a clean O(n) one, and the delicate part is updating that counter only on the exact crossings of the required count, both when adding and when removing, because that is where subtle bugs hide. I also mention that for a fixed alphabet I would use a small integer array rather than a hash map to remove boxing, and that this same fixed-window template directly answers the closely related find-all-anagrams problem just by collecting every start index instead of returning on the first match. Demonstrating that one template covers a family of problems is exactly what interviewers reward.
